title: IECC BOARD MEETING
full_story:
The Board of Trustees of the Illinois Eastern Community College met Tuesday, at Wabash Valley College.

The Board approved the appointment of Esther Cha to fill the open seat on the Board of Trustees.  Susan Batchelor was elected Secretary Pro Tempore.

Approval of employment was given for Marsha Foshee as Math Instructor, Olney Central College effective August 12th; Laura Nead as Math Instructor, Wabash Valley College effective August 12th, James Sigler as STEM Dean of Instruction, Wabash Valley College effective July 27th, Stewart Cramer as Director of Performing Arts, Lincoln Trail College effective July 27th, Paul Manhart as Custodian, Lincoln Trail College effective July 27th, and Theressa Thacker as Custodian, Lincoln Trail College effective July 27th.

Resignation ratifications were approved for Jack Knittle as Math Instructor, Wabash Valley College effective August 4th, Danyelle Ayres as Director of ICAPS and Instruction and Transition, Frontier Community College effective June 30th, and Jesus Gonzales as Head Men’s & Women’s Soccer Coach, Lincoln Trail College effective July 15th.

The next regular meeting of the Board of Trustees will be Tuesday, August 18th, at 6:15 pm at Olney Central College.

title: BLOOD DRIVES
full_story:
The American Red Cross is facing an emergency blood shortage and needs donors to give now and take steps to protect patient care.  A steep decline in blood donations since the end of May has created a growing gap between supply and patient need.  Every donation is critical to rebuilding the nation’s blood supply.

There will be a Blood Drive at the Flora Oddfellows Lodge tomorrow from 1 to 5 pm.  Donors at this drive will get a Fandango Movie Reward by email.

The American Red Cross is asking for blood donations as the supply fell by nearly 25% in June.  Summer is the height of trauma season and the gap between school blood drives, is leaving the Red Cross with a blood shortage.  There are upcoming donation opportunities to help quell what it calls an emergency need.

Red Cross spokesperson Ann Vastmans says there are some common misconceptions about blood donations she would like to address:

The Red Cross cannot “stockpile” blood supply as it has a limited shelf life that must be continually replenished.  Types O positive and B negative blood are especially needed.  Learn more at RedCrossBlood.org/July.

The next blood drive in our area will be on Tuesday, August 11th at the Blue Point Free Will Baptist Church from Noon to 6 pm.  Then on Thursday, August 13th there will be a blood drive at the Flora Church of the Nazarene.  People donating at these drives will get a $20 Amazon Gift Card by email.

title: FMH SCHOOL SPORT PHYSICALS
full_story:
Fairfield Memorial Hospital, in partnership with Horizon Healthcare, will offer school and sports physicals at no cost.

These physicals offer families the opportunity to obtain required school and sports physicals at no out-of-pocket cost.  Horizon Healthcare providers will visit scheduled schools and communities across southern Illinois to conduct the physicals.

The remaining scheduled times include: Clay City on Wednesday, July 29th from 1 pm to 3 pm, and in Flora on Thursday, August 6th from Noon to 5 pm.

Students in Cisne may schedule appointments directly through their local Horizon Healthcare Clinic.

For additional information or to schedule an appointment where required, contact Horizon Healthcare or Fairfield Memorial Hospital.

title: EV CHARGING STATION ONLINE
full_story:
The Illinois Department of Transportation was joined by community leaders in Casey Wednesday to cut the ribbon on the first charging station built in the state through the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Program, with more to come soon.  Additionally, IDOT announced it is awarding $23.5 million through the third round of funding in the program for 29 new projects as part of the effort to build a network of chargers along the interstate system.

Administered by IDOT using federal funds through the Infrastructure Investment & Jobs Act, the state’s NEVI program aims to accelerate the adoption of EVs by providing the public access to fast charging throughout the state, in communications and along interstates, scenic byways.  The program is part of a series of comprehensive initiatives to achieve the state’s goal of becoming a leader in manufacturing and deploying electric vehicles.

In Casey, the first chargers through NEVI in Illinois were electrified last week at the Mach 1 station on Illinois 49 near Interstate 70.  The project built four DC fast chargers, made possible through a $854,641 competitive grant to Phillips 66, in collaboration with Meyer Oil and Electrify America.  Additional station locations will continue coming online this summer.

The $23.5 million in the latest round of grants represents Round 3 of NEVI funding in Illinois and will facilitate the construction of 140 new charging ports.  Each of the 29 locations will have at least four DC fast charging ports to fully charge a typical EV from empty in less than 30 minutes.

title: GRAZING CONFERENCE
full_story:
Decades of grazing innovation on the farm of Curt Rincker in Shelby County was a tour highlight last week during the 24th Heart of America Grazing Conference.

The annual event, which rotates between Kentucky, Missouri, Illinois, Ohio and Indiana, was held in Effingham this year and bussed nearly 100 people to tour Rincker’s farm.  There, attendees learned about pasture management, regenerative grazing for both large and small ruminants and Environmental Quality Incentive Program projects including the farm’s spring-fed watering system and winter feeding station.

“In the mid-90s, I started thinking I didn’t have enough hay to meet my cattle needs, so I began some efforts with (University of Illinois) Extension adviser Ed Ballard and Larry Casey and we established a grazing program that at that time was kind of innovative,” Rincker told Rita Frazer with the RFD Radio Network.  It included 10 pastures where cattle were rotated every three to four days.

During the tour, Ballard discussed some of the studies that were done on the farm in the past 25 years, including how body intake increased from 2% of body weight up to as high as 5%, which transformed into higher rate of gain and feed efficiency.

Standing in the pasture, Rincker explained how there is a lot of fescue grass in his area that often goes through a “summer slump” this time of year.

“We learned to spring-frost-seed red clover to try to get to more legumes, we try to spot spray and either harvest the pastures off or top the heads out before they develop the endophyte fungus from the fescue,” Rincker said.  “We also learned that cattle will kind of tell you when it’s time to move, and so you watch their behavior and learn from them as well.”

Logan Karcher, director of producer programs for the Illinois Grazing Lands Coalition (ILGLC), said hosting the tour in Illinois was an opportunity to spotlight ways to utilize cattle on crop ground.

“Something that we really promote is regenerative grazing, adaptive grazing and getting the animals back on the land to help our soil health,” he told FarmWeek.

During the two-day event, attendees also heard presentations about grazing-related research from the University of Illinois, genetics and virtual fencing, a tool of growing interest for rotational graziers.

Rick Adams of Kankakee County, Terry Becherer of Clinton County and Perry Hottes of Jefferson County were recognized as ILGLC 2026 Master Graziers during the event.

title: CYCLOSPORIASIS CASES
full_story:
Officials say the confirmed number of cyclosporiasis cases linked to an ongoing outbreak could be higher than 11,000.  The CDC provided a recent update announcing that over 4,000 cases have been linked to the outbreak across 41 states.

According to officials, “many of the additional cases have been reported by Michigan and Ohio,” but the FDA maintains that while dozens of states are impacted, the outbreak investigation has been predominately linked to “at least” five states: Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, West Virginia and Kentucky.  Other states such as North Carolina and Kansas have also seen a recent spike in cases.  Cyclosporiasis cases are typically reported between May and August each year, but it is usually only a handful or a few dozen.

In Illinois, there have been more than 400 cases of Cyclosporiasis.  According to the IDPH 145 cases were reported from people who traveled outside the US, 215 were acquired domestically and 48 cases have unknown origins.  Out of the 408 confirmed and probable cases, the IDPH said there have been 31 hospitalizations.

title: ISP VEHICLE THEFT DETAIL
full_story:
The Illinois State Police (ISP) continues to target vehicle theft, hijacking, and related violent crimes using grant funding from the Illinois Secretary of State Illinois Vehicle Hijacking and Motor Vehicle Theft Prevention and Insurance Verification Council.  ISP was awarded a $10 million grant for the first fiscal year, another $677,000 in June 2024, and $637,500 in July 2025.

title: HYUNDAI RECALL
full_story:
Hyundai is recalling over 47,000 Kona SUVs for a defect with the rear center seat belt.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says the recall covers nearly 48,000 vehicles, including certain 2025 Hyundai Kona Electric and 2026 Hyundai Kona model.  The automaker said the rear center seat belt buckle may fail to properly restrain a passenger during a crash.  Hyundai is advising owners not to use the rear center seating position until its repaired.

According to recall documents, Hyundai’s supplier, Joyson Safety Systems, notified the automaker in February that testing identified a potential problem with the rear center seat belt buckle used in the Kona.

Joyson determined the issue may have resulted from inadequate inspection controls that allowed metal stamping dies used to manufacture the buckles to remain in service beyond their intended lifespan, leading to excessive wear.

Although there have been no confirmed crashes, injuries, fires or other incidents related to the issue, Hyundai said it decided to conduct the recall “out of an abundance of caution.”

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed September 11th and dealers will replace the rear center seat buckle assembly free of charge.

title: BLUE ENVELOPE PROGRAM
full_story:
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announced that Illinois will launch a statewide Blue Envelope Program, following the recent signing of legislation into law.

The new voluntary program is designed to improve communication and reduce stress during traffic stops for drivers with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) while providing law enforcement with a simple tool to enhance safety and understanding.

The Blue Envelope Program will be administered by the Secretary of State’s office in partnership with law enforcement agencies and autism advocacy organizations.  Blue envelopes will be available free of charge at DMVs and participating police departments throughout Illinois.

The program allows drivers, passengers or vehicle owners to keep their driver’s license, vehicle registration and proof of insurance inside a distinctive blue envelope.  When presented during a traffic stop, the envelope serves as an immediate visual cue that the individual may benefit from additional patience or different communication techniques.

The envelope will also contain practical guidance for both drivers and law enforcement, including communication tips, preferred methods of communication and space for emergency contact information.

While several Illinois law enforcement agencies already participate in local Blue Envelope programs through partnerships with autism advocacy organizations, the new law creates the first consistent statewide program, ensuring families and officers have access to the same resources regardless of where they live or travel in Illinois.

The Secretary of State’s office has developed a standardized blue envelope in consultation with the Autism Hero Project.

Law enforcement agencies, fire departments and other participating organizations will be able to request blue envelopes through the Secretary of State’s office as part of its services for people with disabilities.

The Blue Envelope Program complements existing Illinois disability accommodations, including voluntary disability designations associated with driver records and vehicle registrations, by providing an immediate, visible communication tool during traffic stops.  Unlike the Illinois Person with a Disability Identification Card and Disability Wallet Card, no medical certification or documentation is required to receive a blue envelope.

The Blue Envelope Program originated in Connecticut in 2020 and has expanded rapidly nationwide.  Today, nearly 20 states – and hundreds of municipalities, including dozens in Illinois – have implemented or proposed similar programs to improve interactions between law enforcement and individuals with autism.

Additional information about obtaining blue envelopes and participating in the program will be announced before the law takes effect on January 1st.
